nodes.title: ServiceNow Update Sets: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Update Sets are the unit of deployment in ServiceNow, capturing configuration changes made in one instance so they can be transported and applied to another (e.g., dev → test → production).

flashcards.front: What does an Update Set capture?
flashcards.back: Configuration changes to the ServiceNow platform (scripts, UI policies, workflows, business rules, etc.) but NOT data records or instance-specific attachments.

flashcards.front: Update Set states: In Progress → Complete → workflow?
flashcards.back: Set the Update Set to Complete to prevent further changes, then retrieve it in the target instance and Preview to check for conflicts before Committing.

flashcards.front: What happens during Preview in the target instance?
flashcards.back: ServiceNow compares the incoming Update Set against the target's current state and flags conflicts or missing records so you can resolve them before commit.

flashcards.front: Batch Update Set — what is it?
flashcards.back: A parent container grouping multiple Update Sets so they can be transported, previewed, and committed together in the correct order.

questions.q: A ServiceNow administrator needs to promote custom configurations (Business Rules, UI Policies, form layouts) from the Development instance to Production. What is the correct mechanism?
choices: Export the database and import it into the Production instance
Use the ServiceNow Store to publish configurations from Development to Production
Package configuration changes in an Update Set.
Re-create all configurations manually in the Production instance
questions.explanation: Update Sets are containers that capture configuration changes (Business Rules, UI Policies, Client Scripts, workflows, form layouts, etc.) made while the Update Set is active. You export the Update Set as an XML file from Development, import it into Production, preview it for conflicts, then commit it. Note: Update Sets do NOT capture data records (incidents, users) — only configuration metadata. export it from Development, and import/commit it in Production

questions.q: A company's ServiceNow system property 'glide.ui.activity.stream.enabled' needs to be changed in Production. A junior admin changes it directly in Production without using an Update Set. What problem does this create?
choices: No problem — system properties are environment-specific and changed without Update Sets intentionally, as they do not need to be replicated

The property change will be automatically reverted without an Update Set during the next ServiceNow upgrade — upgrades do not revert property changes; the risk is that the change is not captured and cannot be replicated

ServiceNow automatically creates an Update Set for all system property changes made without manual intervention — ServiceNow does not auto-capture property changes into Update Sets; changes made without an Update Set are not tracked
System properties changed without an Update Set are not captured and cannot be easily replicated
questions.explanation: System properties changed outside an active Update Set are not captured in any Update Set. This means: the change cannot be documented or rolled back via Update Sets, and if Production needs to be restored or a similar change needs to be made in Dev/Test, it must be done manually. Best practice is always to make configuration changes (including system properties) while an Update Set is active in the appropriate environment.

questions.q: A company is going live with ServiceNow ITSM for the first time. The project team asks what data should NOT be transported via Update Sets when migrating configuration from Development to Production.
choices: Data records such as user accounts.
Form layouts and list view configurations
Business Rules, Client Scripts, and UI Policies
questions.explanation: Update Sets capture metadata/configuration changes (Business Rules, Workflows, form layouts, etc.) but NOT data records. User accounts, groups, incidents, service catalog request records, and environment-specific system properties (URLs, passwords, credentials) should NOT be transported via Update Sets. Data migration requires separate tools (data import with Import Sets, manual configuration per environment, or Automated Test Framework). groups, existing incidents, catalog items' variable values, and system properties with environment-specific values

questions.q: A ServiceNow project is about to go live. The UAT team discovers that 3 of the 50 Update Set changes conflict with an existing customization in the Test instance. What is the recommended approach?
choices: Commit all Update Sets ignoring conflicts and fix issues in the Production instance after go-live — committing without previewing on the Test instance risks breaking production configurations

Delete all conflicting Update Sets and rebuild affected configurations from scratch in the Production instance — destructive approach; the Test instance preview step exists to identify and resolve conflicts safely

Merge all Update Sets into a single batch Update Set to avoid individual conflicts without previewing in the Test instance — merging does not resolve conflicts; each Update Set should be previewed in the Test instance first
Preview each Update Set in the Test instance.
questions.explanation: The correct Update Set deployment process is: (1) Load/upload the Update Set XML into the target instance, (2) Preview the Update Set — ServiceNow identifies potential conflicts and shows a preview log, (3) Resolve conflicts (decide which version of conflicting records to use), (4) Commit. This preview step is critical — never skip it in Production. Update Sets with unresolved conflicts can overwrite important configurations. review the conflicts in the Preview log, resolve them (choose which version to keep), then commit in the correct order

nodes.title: Mixed exam topics: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Some exam objectives don't fit neatly into a single domain — they span protocols, tools, or concepts covered briefly in multiple sections. These cards treat each item as a stand-alone fact, the way an exam question presents it: one concept, one answer.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a hub, a switch, and a router?
flashcards.back: Hub: Layer 1, repeats every frame to all ports — all devices share bandwidth, collisions guaranteed. Switch: Layer 2, forwards frames using a MAC address table to only the destination port — full duplex, no collisions, each port gets full bandwidth. Router: Layer 3, makes forwarding decisions based on IP address, connects different networks. Hub is legacy; switches dominate LAN; routers are at network edges.

flashcards.front: What is RAID 5 and how many drives can it tolerate losing?
flashcards.back: RAID 5 stripes data and parity across at least 3 drives. Any single drive failure can be recovered by reconstructing missing data from the remaining drives and parity. It cannot tolerate 2 simultaneous drive failures. Effective capacity = (N-1) × drive size. Read performance is excellent; write requires parity recalculation. RAID 6 tolerates 2 failures using double parity.

flashcards.front: What does a proxy server do, and how does a forward proxy differ from a reverse proxy?
flashcards.back: Forward proxy: sits between clients and the internet on behalf of clients — used for content filtering, caching, and anonymizing outbound requests (the server sees the proxy's IP). Reverse proxy: sits in front of servers on behalf of the server — used for load balancing, SSL termination, caching, and hiding backend topology (the client sees the proxy's IP). Both intermediate HTTP, but they protect opposite sides.

flashcards.front: What is the purpose of a DMZ in network architecture?
flashcards.back: A demilitarized zone is a network segment between the untrusted internet and the trusted internal network, typically protected by two firewalls (or two interfaces on one firewall). Public-facing services (web, email, DNS) sit in the DMZ: internet can reach them but not the internal network; if the DMZ host is compromised, the inner firewall still blocks access to the internal LAN.
